title: The tongue (James 3:1–12)
hook: a small rudder, a small spark: the tongue sets forests on fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and works, warm words at a closed door, and your line was faith that works.

A wildfire can start from almost nothing. A spark from a dragged chain. One cigarette. A campfire left smoldering. A few days later the smoke is visible from space, and whole towns are packing their cars. Investigators sometimes trace the fire back to a single point on the ground, small enough to cover with your hand. James never saw a satellite photo, but he knew what a small fire can do, and he used it to describe something that sits in every mouth.

He starts with a warning to teachers. Not many of you should become teachers, he says, because teachers will be judged more strictly. People who talk for a living have more to answer for. Then three pictures of small things steering big ones. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A huge ship, driven by fierce winds, is "turned about with a very small helm," the rudder, wherever the pilot wants. And then: "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" That word matter is a puzzle in English. The Greek word means wood, or forest. How great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. The bit and the rudder steer. The spark destroys. Then something that stings: people have tamed every kind of animal, birds and snakes and sea creatures, "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." And the line that turns it inward: "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be." With the tongue, James says, we bless God, and with it we curse people made in God's likeness. Praise on Sunday, cursing by Monday. Does a spring pour fresh water and bitter from the same opening? Can a fig tree grow olives? He isn't saying never speak. He's saying words are fire. They can warm a house or burn it down, and the same mouth does both.
screen: then, large: `HOW GREAT A MATTER A LITTLE FIRE KINDLETH!`

segments.voice: Think back to the last unkind thing you said, out loud or in a text, and without punishing yourself, picture it like a spark landing in dry grass. Then picture the moment today you're most likely to say something sharp, and your mouth staying closed, or opening with something else after a breath. If you pray, you can ask for a guard on your mouth.
The tongue. For James, a small part of the body that steers like a rudder and burns like a spark, and that no one can fully tame.
Your line: a small fire. One spark, one forest. Day six hundred seventy-four, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians include their speech in a daily or weekly self-examination, and churches turn to James 3 when teaching about gossip, anger and online behavior.

chat.says: Words are just words. Why does James make such a big deal about them?
options: He says the tongue is small but steers like a rudder and burns like a spark.
He says only teachers need to worry; everyone else's words matter little.
He says it's fine to curse people as long as you also praise God.
chat.meaning: "How great a matter a little fire kindleth!": for James, the tongue is a little member that can steer, or set a forest ablaze.

γλῶσσα and English 'gloss/glossary': standard etymology. Confirm.
